title-group.article-title: Patterns of neurotoxicity among patients receiving chimeric antigen receptor T‐cell therapy: A single‐centre cohort study

sec.title: Background and purpose
sec.p: Immune effector cell‐associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) is an important complication of chimeric antigen receptor T‐cell (CAR‐T) therapy. This study aims to identify the patterns of neurotoxicity among patients with ICANS at a tertiary referral centre in Australia.

sec.title: Methodology
sec.p: This single‐centre, prospective cohort study included all consecutively recruited patients who underwent CAR‐T therapy for eligible haematological malignancies. All patients underwent a comprehensive neurological assessment and cognitive screening before CAR‐T infusion, during the development of ICANS, and 1 month after treatment. Baseline demographic characteristics, incidence, and neurological patterns of neurotoxicity management were evaluated.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Over a 19‐month period, 23% (12) of the 53 eligible patients developed neurotoxicity (10/12 [83%] being grade 1). All patients showed changes in handwriting and tremor as their initial presentation. Changes in cognition were manifested in most of the patients, with a more substantial drop noted in their Montreal Cognitive Assessment compared to immune effector cell‐associated encephalopathy scores. All manifestations of neurotoxicity were short‐lived and resolved within a 1‐month period, with a mean duration of 8.2 days (range = 1–33).

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The patterns of CAR‐T‐related neurotoxicity often include change in handwriting, tremor, and mild confusional state, especially early in their evolution. These may remain undetected by routine neurological surveillance. These features represent accessible clinical markers of incipient ICANS.
Keywords: axicabtagene ciloleucel, CAR‐T therapy, ICANS, neurotoxicity, tisagenlecleucel

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Immune effector cell‐associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) is the second most common complication of chimeric antigen receptor T‐cell (CAR‐T) therapy. In clinical trials, moderate to severe ICANS was reported in 30%–60% of subjects, whereas most recent studies have documented lower rates (19%–21%) [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. The mortality rate from neurotoxicity is low (0%–1.4%) [4, 5, 6], but recognition of its early signs is essential, as patients with moderate to severe disease often endure prolonged hospitalization and increased morbidity.

The most common presentation of ICANS involves cognitive impairment, ranging from acute confusional states to severe encephalopathy [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. Although the immune effector cell‐associated encephalopathy (ICE) scoring system is a validated and concise method of assessing neurotoxicity, it may not capture subtle and early changes. For example, confusion and irritability may manifest as early as 30 h prior to a drop in ICE scores [8]. Tremor and handwriting changes may also be early manifestations of ICANS [7]. Information about the early symptomatology of ICANS is scarce, yet important to recognize, as early treatment has been shown to improve clinical outcomes [9]. Corticosteroids are the mainstay of treatment, but recent studies demonstrate that its liberal use may alter the CAR‐T kinematics, affecting its efficacy [9, 10, 11].

In this study, we describe the early manifestations of neurotoxicity among patients receiving CAR‐T therapy for haematological neoplasms, monitored with a comprehensive neurological protocol at a single Australian tertiary referral centre.

sec.title: METHODOLOGY
sec.p: This is single‐centre, prospective cohort study includes all consecutively recruited patients who underwent CAR‐T therapy for relapsed diffuse large B‐cell lymphoma (DLBCL) multiple myeloma or mediastinal lymphoma at the Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre in Melbourne, Australia between 1 February 2021 and 31 August 2022. Patients with involvement of the central nervous system were also included. Only patients receiving standard‐of‐care CAR‐T products, including tisagenlecleucel or axicabtagene ciloleucel, outside clinical trials, were included in this study. Treatment decision was made by the treating haematologist with consideration of the patient's oncologic burden and neurologic profile. Only patients 18 years or older and able to read and write were included.

Structured standard neurological examination was followed by cognitive screening with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). A comprehensive neuropsychologic examination was performed separately. Assessments were performed at several predefined time points, namely: (i) baseline (prior to lymphodepletion chemotherapy), (ii) 1 month following CAR‐T infusion, and (iii) at any point following infusion when neurotoxicity was suspected. The diagnosis of ICANS was made following the American Society of Transplantation and Cellular Therapy (ASTCT) definition of progressive neurologic symptoms. This includes aphasia, altered conscious state, cognitive impairment, weakness, seizures, and signs of increased intracranial pressure in the context of CAR‐T therapy [12]. Importantly, nonspecific symptoms such as headache, hallucinations, and hyperkinetic movement disorders (tremor, myoclonus, and asterixis) are not considered diagnostic of ICANS [12]. The degree of neurotoxicity was quantified with the 10‐point ICE score. The treatment decisions in patients with ICANS were made based on a consensus between the treating haematologists, neurologists, and neuropsychologists. All patients with ICANS underwent cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Electroencephalography (EEG) and lumbar puncture were performed in all patients with moderate to severe ICANS and in some of the patients mild ICANS.

Monitoring of severity of stable ICANS was performed by regular 8‐hourly clinical assessments with re‐evaluation of ICE. The frequency is increased to every 30 min for patients who are at a high risk of neurological deterioration. Grade 1 neurotoxicity is managed on a standard ward, whereas intensive care unit (ICU) admission is considered for grade 2 ICANS. Grade 3 and 4 neurotoxicity is managed in the ICU. At our centre, treatment is initiated in all patients with ICANS, including mild cases. Patients with grade 1 neurotoxicity are treated with boluses of dexamethasone 4–10 mg iv as required. Regular 6‐hourly dexamethasone 10 mg iv is administered to patients with grade 2 to 4 neurotoxicity. High‐dose methylprednisolone (500–1000 mg iv) is considered in severe and refractory ICANS. Anakinra (100 mg sc every 12 h) is reserved for patients with severe ICANS refractory to corticosteroid treatment. Other treatment options, particularly for steroid‐refractory ICANS, include cyclophosphamide and plasma exchange. Prophylactic antiseizure medication (ASM) with nonsedating properties such as levetiracetam is recommended for all patients with grade 2–4 neurotoxicity and can be considered in grade 1 neurotoxicity. We also consider a short course of ASM prophylaxis prior to CAR‐T infusion for patients who are at a high risk for neurotoxicity, to continue for 2–4 weeks postinfusion.

sec.title: Data acquisition and evaluation
sec.p: Baseline demographic characteristics and clinical features were recorded in a structured database (RedCap). The electronic database was stored and maintained on a secure hospital server at the Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre. This study was approved by the Peter MacCallum Human Ethics Committee.

We recorded a full personal or family history of neurological or psychological diagnoses. Important neurological features documented include use of gait aids and history of visual, speech, and hearing impairment, along with any history of tremors and peripheral neuropathy. We also captured all current medications and history of smoking and alcohol consumption. In relation to the presenting haematological diagnosis, we documented disease duration, central nervous system (CNS) involvement, previous treatments including bridging therapies, and any neurological and neuropsychological complications related to prior therapies received. Neurological information was structured as shown in the Supplement. The structured neurological assessment captured all aspects of neurological function following neurological systems, including the Medical Research Council assessment of muscle strength. Tremor laterality, frequency, severity, and symmetry were evaluated. Handwriting and Archimedean spiral were assessed periodically. Cognitive screening with the MoCA was performed for all patients. This is a descriptive study; the patient characteristics were summarized with mean, SD, and range, median and quartiles, or as percentages, as appropriate.

sec.title: RESULTS
sec.p: Over a 19‐month period, 79 patients undergoing CAR‐T therapy for haematological indications completed baseline neurological assessment at the Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre. We excluded 26 patients who were enrolled in randomized clinical trials. A total of 53 patients were considered eligible (Figure 1).

sec.p: Twelve patients (23%) developed neurotoxicity during the studied period. The majority of patients developed grade 1 neurotoxicity (10/12, 83%), whereas only two patients (17%) developed grade 3 neurotoxicity. No treatment‐related deaths were recorded. Nine (75%) of the patients who developed neurotoxicity were males. The mean age of patients included in our study was 62.1 years (range = 34–74 years). In three patients (25%), a history of neurological disease predating the haematological malignancy or CAR‐T therapy was reported (meningioma, transient ischemic attack, and mild traumatic brain injury). A history of neurological symptoms related to chemotherapy included peripheral neuropathy (33% of the included patients), tremor (17%), depression (25%), and anxiety (25%).

Patients who received CAR‐T therapy and developed ICANS had either DLBCL/high‐grade B‐cell lymphoma (11 patients, 91.7%) or primary CNS lymphoma (1 patient, 8.3%). The mean time from the initial haematological diagnosis to the CAR‐T therapy was 3.8 years (range = 1–10.3 years). Of the patients who developed ICANS, three (25%) had a history of haematological CNS involvement by the primary malignancy, including two (16.6%) with a residual CNS disease at the time of CAR‐T infusion. In comparison, three of the 41 patients (0.07%) who did not develop ICANS had a history of CNS involvement due to the haematological malignancy. All patients underwent standard first‐ and second‐line chemotherapy prior to CAR‐T therapy, whereas radiotherapy and stem cell transplant were performed in six (50%) and three (25%) of patients who developed ICANS, respectively. Ten of our patients underwent baseline neuroimaging, which confirmed haematological CNS involvement in two (20%) patients. Ten (83%) of the patients who developed ICANS received axicabtagene ciloleucel (Yescarta), whereas the remaining two (17%) were treated with tisagenlecleucel (Kymriah).

Of the patients who developed ICANS, 11 patients (91.6%) had developed mild to moderate cytokine release syndrome (CRS). More than 50% of the patients had CRS grade 2 followed by 25% who had grade 1 and only 1 (8.5%) who developed grade 3 CRS. In comparison, 26 of the 41 patients (63.4%) who did not develop ICANS experienced CRS. Cranial MRI was performed in 10 of the 12 patients with ICANS during the acute deterioration of their neurological status. Seven scans showed normal results, two scans showed changes likely related to ICANS, and one scan showed nonspecific findings that predated CAR‐T therapy. The findings related to ICANS included transient diffusion restriction in the cerebellum and T2/fluid‐attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintense lesions in the right pontine region (Figure 2a,b). EEG was performed in six patients while they were symptomatic with ICANS. The most common abnormal EEG finding was generalized slowing documented in three patients, whereas normal EEG was reported in two patients. Frontal intermittent rhythmic delta activity was reported in one patient with grade 1 neurotoxicity. No epileptiform discharges were recorded in this cohort. Lumbar puncture was completed in two patients. Abnormal cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was reported in both of our grade 3 neurotoxicity patients, including elevation of CSF protein in both patients and mild pleocytosis in one patient. The infective screen yielded negative results, and cytology and flow cytometry did not show any evidence of malignant cells or CAR‐Ts in the CSF. Eleven of our patients received corticosteroid treatment during the first drop in their ICE score. The mean cumulative dose of dexamethasone (in either intravenous or oral form) was 34.6 mg (range = 0–114 mg). Three patients commenced levetiracetam for seizure prophylaxis (one patient with primary CNS lymphoma and two patients with grade 3 neurotoxicity). One patient received anakinra for refractory ICANS. sec.p: Table 2 outlines the individual characteristics of the 12 patients who developed ICANS. The patient with the most prominent neurological findings (Patient 5)—which included changes in handwriting, attention, following commands, orientation, and naming and severe tremor—developed CRS grade 3 followed by ICANS grade 3, with an ICE of 1 at the nadir of the presentation. The patient was treated with a cumulative dose of dexamethasone of 114 mg and prophylactic levetiracetam and recovered after 30 days. Changes in handwriting were observed among all patients at the baseline. In those with mild neurotoxicity, the impaired handwriting presented with dysgraphia and micrographia, whereas those patients who developed grade 3 ICANS exhibited ideomotor apraxia, agraphia, and paligraphia (Figure 2c,d).

sec.p: All patients with abnormal handwriting also developed distal upper extremity tremor, mostly postural and kinetic, bilateral, 7–8 Hz, and small amplitude, and one patient manifested with bilateral facial tremor. Two of the patients who had a previous history of tremor experienced worsening of their tremor during ICANS, whereas in 10 patients the onset of tremor was new. One patient presented with myoclonic jerks with no impairment of awareness and without epileptiform discharges on EEG.

Of the included patients, 77.4% did not show any new abnormal findings on neurological examination after receiving CAR‐T therapy. Changes of gait have been observed in some patients, primarily due to deconditioning during hospitalization, and none showed overt cerebellar, pyramidal, or extrapyramidal signs or sensory changes.

On screening of cognitive function, we observed subnormal performance in all patients with ICANS as per their MoCA scores (or ICE scores in three patients for whom MoCA scores were not available). Overall, there was a mean 4.1 (range = 1–6) point decline in MoCA scores during neurotoxicity, but this reverted to baseline 1 month after CAR‐T therapy. Interestingly, both patients with and without cognitive impairment reported in their ICE scores showed transient decline in their MoCA scores during ICANS (Figure 3), with grade 3 neurotoxicity having significant ideomotor and constructional apraxia, anomia, and disorientation.

sec.p: Figure 4 represents the individual trajectories of patients with neurotoxicity secondary to CAR‐T therapy. ICANS was diagnosed at an average of 8.6 days (range = 6–12) after CAR‐T infusion, with a mean duration of 8.2 days (range = 1–33). All but one patient had CRS preceding the diagnosis of ICANS. Interestingly, we observed that all patients developed tremor, at an average of 7.2 days (range = 3–12) after infusion, before or at the first decline in their ICE score.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: This study describes the patterns of neurotoxicity, based on the clinical experience at the largest CAR‐T program in Australia. The incidence of any ICANS recorded in our cohort is 23%, with grade 3 neurotoxicity accounting for only 4%. In comparison to the numbers documented in clinical trials and other observational studies, the incidence of any or moderate to severe neurotoxicity is lower in our cohort [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. In our cohort, nearly 50% of patients did not show any signs of cognitive impairment in their ICE scores, but all of them had a decline in their MoCA scores, with concomitant subtle dysexecutive syndrome on neuropsychologic evaluation, consistent with other studies [13]. Only two of our patients developed grade 3 neurotoxicity, with significant ideational and ideomotor apraxia, acalculia, and dysexecutive syndrome. Further assessments of their handwriting revealed agrammatism and repetition of the same letter consistent with paligraphia. This handwriting pattern was also previously reported as an early feature of neurotoxicity by Pensato et al. [14]. On the other hand, all our patients with grade 1 neurotoxicity had mild micrographia compared to baseline. Interestingly, all of them had action‐related tremors, and whether these handwriting changes are related to this remains speculative. Language dysfunction seems to be a less prominent feature of our ICANS patients, regardless of severity. This is contrary to another study, where patients with neurotoxicity had language impairment in the form of echolalia, reduced fluency, and dysphasia [14]. Reports of verbal perseveration, global aphasia, and mutism have also been described in severe cases [15, 16]. Most of the patients also developed a brief period of cognitive dysfunction with associated impairments in speed processing, visuospatial function, and attention and delayed recall noted in their MoCA scores. Notably, among patients who only dropped 1 point for handwriting changes in their ICE scores, a greater drop in their MoCA was observed, with predominant deficits in attention and language. Although the ICE score is a practical tool for assessing neurotoxicity among CAR‐T patients, it may underestimate the degree of neurocognitive dysfunction.

Motor and cranial nerve involvement after CAR‐T therapy is also uncommon. We did not observe any evidence of cranial neuropathies or focal weakness among our patients, although generalized weakness may occur over a short period in the setting of nonneurologic causes such as CRS, infections, and fatigue. Few cases of cranial neuropathies were reported in patients receiving axicabtagene ciloleucel in the ZUMA‐1 trial, but the recent CARTITUDE 4 trial involving more than 400 patients who had cilta‐cel infusion for multiple myeloma reported 16 (9.1%) cases of craniopathies [17, 18]. None of the patients included in this study received the latter. In a study by Rubin and colleagues, focal weakness was observed in 11% of patients, with most being transient, lasting for a few hours to days [7]. Three cases of myelopathy have also been reported in literature, with two being refractory to high‐dose intravenous steroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, anakinra (in one patient), and siltuximab (in another) [17, 19, 20]. Although the ASTCT defines ICANS to be a phenomenon involving the CNS, reports of peripheral nerve involvement have also been described. Two cases of Guillain–Barré syndrome have been reported following cilta‐cel and tisa‐cel infusion [21, 22]. Motor presentations can vary from lower motor to upper motor neuron presentation, hence the need to recognize early signs and its pattern to institute early intervention.

All our ICANS patients developed tremors, which are typically posture‐ or action‐related, nearly symmetric bilaterally, low amplitude, and moderate in frequency and usually involve the upper extremities. The work of Rubin et al. previously highlighted that the earliest manifestations of neurotoxicity in their cohort were hyperkinetic movement disorders such as tremors, asterixis, and myoclonus [7]. This is consistent with our findings, where tremors occurred at an average of 1 day prior to the first drop in their ICE scores. Hyperkinetic movements such as tremor, asterixis, and myoclonus, however, are not diagnostic of ICANS according to the 2019 ASTCT guidelines [12]. It is likely a neurologic manifestation of a systemic hormonal alteration such as disruption in the catecholaminergic response triggered by CRS [23].

Standard neurologic investigations for ICANS include MRI, EEG, and CSF analysis, and nerve conduction studies may be necessary in certain scenarios. Only two of 10 MRIs were noted to be abnormal in our cohort, with findings of diffusion restriction in the cerebellum in one and T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the brainstem in the other. Most studies confirm that there is no specific neuroradiologic signature for patients with ICANS [10, 23, 24, 25]. Some of the abnormal findings noted in another study include features consistent with encephalitis, stroke, leptomeningeal disease, and posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome [10]. Our team proposed that MRI‐related neurotoxicity abnormalities be classified according to anatomical (white matter, grey matter, brainstem, and leptomeninges) and pathological (ischaemia, haemorrhage involvement) involvement [24]. Consistent with other studies, the neuroimaging features of neurotoxicity appear to improve following steroid therapy [26]. The likely mechanism is the disruption of the blood–brain barrier resulting from endothelial activation and a cytokine surge from CAR‐T expansion [27].

EEG is another useful paraclinical tool, as the most common symptom of ICANS is encephalopathy and, in severe cases, status epilepticus. The most common EEG pattern observed in our cohort is generalized slowing, with grade 1 ICANS patients having background activity in the alpha to theta range, whereas the two patients with grade 3 neurotoxicity had more severe slowing in the delta–theta range, consistent with the findings in paediatric and adult patients, wherein background frequency correlated with the severity of neurotoxicity [27, 28]. Focal EEG patterns are not uncommon in patients with ICANS, with one study demonstrating that 27% of patients had focal EEG patterns consistent with lateralized periodic discharges, lateralized rhythmic delta activity, and focal slowing [29].

CSF is likewise an important differential diagnostic marker. Mild pleocytosis is commonly observed among patients with neurotoxicity, although no correlation between CSF cell counts or the quantity of CAR‐Ts and the severity of ICANS has been established [30]. Proinflammatory cytokines such as IL6, IL8, MCP1, and IP10, however, were noted to be disproportionately elevated in the CSF compared to serum, which may be suggestive of its intrathecal synthesis [30]. Whether these biomarkers may have utility in the diagnosis and prognostication of ICANS needs further validation in large‐scale studies.

At our centre, patients with grade 1 ICANS are treated with steroids, in contrast to published recommendations, where steroids are only administered among those who deteriorate to grade 2 or 3 [31]. This is likely one of the reasons a significantly low number of patients with high‐grade neurotoxicity is noted in our cohort. There is a question, however, concerning the liberal and early use of corticosteroids, as it may reduce the efficacy of CAR‐T therapy. Previous studies have demonstrated that overall and progression‐free survival was lower among patients who received a higher cumulative steroid dose, which is thought to be a result of dose‐dependent destabilization in the equilibrium between CAR‐Ts and the tumour cells [10, 11, 32]. On the other hand, some patients enrolled in the ZUMA‐1 trial received a total of 30 mg prophylactic dexamethasone prior to CAR‐T therapy and maintained high rates of complete response to CAR‐T therapy [9]. This dose, however, was significantly lower than the cumulative steroid doses used in the other two studies.

There is also uncertainty about the role of prophylactic ASMs among patients treated with CAR‐T therapy. Not all our patients with grade 1 ICANS received prophylactic ASM, in contrast to the practice at some other centres [33]. A similarly selective approach is suggested by Cohen and colleagues, who only recommend treatment of grade ≥2 ICANS with prophylactic antiseizure therapies [34]. Using this approach, we have not observed any patients with clinical or electrographic seizures. The most widely recommended ASM is levetiracetam, mainly because of its nonsedative properties, and benzodiazepines, phenobarbital, and lacosamide may be added on in seizures refractory to monotherapy [33]. Our practice is to maintain a prophylactic regimen only over the short term, with discontinuation 14–28 days after hospital discharge.

To date, we have not documented any delayed onset neurotoxicity occurring >30 days from CAR‐T therapy. In general, delayed ICANS is rare except for patients on B‐cell maturation antigen (BCMA) CAR‐T therapy, where movement‐ and neurocognitive treatment‐emergent adverse events up to 3 months after CAR‐Ts were present in 5% [34].

Our study has several limitations. The small number of patients, treated in a single‐site program (albeit the largest in Australia), limits the spectrum of captured clinical scenarios. The lack of a comparator group also limits the generalizability of our findings. Access to BCMA CAR‐T therapy is limited to clinical trials at our institution, and hence was not included in this study.

sec.title: FUTURE PERSPECTIVES
sec.p: Considering the limited understanding of the potential clinical and biochemical markers of ICANS, our future goal is to develop accessible prognostic markers of neurotoxicity following CAR‐T therapy. Long‐term neurological and cognitive outcomes among patients treated with CAR‐T therapy represent an important question that will require cohorts with long‐term follow‐up.
